undoes a commit by adding a new one that reverses its changes, so the undo travels like any other commit. Reset is for work that hasn't left your machine; revert is for work that has.
Lina pushes a debug flag that gives every customer free shipping, and notices a few minutes later. She runs
, Git rejects her push, so she forces it, and the flag disappears from
. That afternoon Omar, who had pulled before the reset, pushes his coupon work as usual. The flag is back on
, and nobody put it there on purpose.
is how you undo a commit, pushed or not. Move the branch back to before the mistake, push, and the mistake is gone for everyone.
It's an understandable belief, because reset really does undo commits. Pro Git's "Reset Demystified" chapter walks through
and points out that it "essentially undid the last git commit command." Afterwards your own
looks perfect: the bad commit is simply not there.
The half-truth is in the word "your". Reset undoes the commit in your repository. It can't reach the copies that already left it.
Pro Git is precise about it: "reset moves the branch that HEAD is pointing to." That's step one, and

goes on to overwrite your working files too. Git's own overview of the commands sums up what all three have in common: reset "is about updating your branch, moving the tip in order to add or remove commits from the branch. This operation changes the commit history."
Other clones still have the commit
A reset changes one pointer in one repository. The commit you "removed" still exists in every clone that pulled it, and their branches still point past it. That's why the
docs, right after an example that drops three commits with
, add: "Do not do this if you have already given these commits to somebody else." Removing a pushed commit also takes a
, which the previous article in this path covered.
Revert records the undo as a new commit

works the other way. Given existing commits, it will "revert the changes that the related patches introduce, and record some new commits that record them." Nothing is rewritten: the revert is an ordinary commit on top, so it pulls and pushes like any other, and the history shows both the mistake and its fix.
Locally, reset is safe, and the reflog has your back
records "when the tips of branches and other references were updated in the local repository", so a commit you reset away is still easy to find. On Git 2.54:

blocks.code:
git reset --hard HEAD~1
# HEAD is now at e88fe03 Add debug free-shipping flag
git reflog -2
# e88fe03 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
# da7f63f HEAD@{1}: commit: Add coupon field
git reset --hard 'HEAD@{1}'
# HEAD is now at da7f63f Add coupon field

content.text: The reflog is local and doesn't last forever: by default,
drops entries after 90 days, or after 30 days when the branch's current tip can no longer reach them.
The fix: revert what's been pushed
Both sessions start from the same history: Lina pushed the flag, and Omar pulled it and committed his own work on top before anyone noticed.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
# Lina
git reset --hard HEAD~1
# HEAD is now at f938e68 Add checkout
git push --force   # a plain push was rejected
#  + 156eb4a...f938e68 main -> main (forced update)
# Omar, later that day
git pull --no-rebase
#  + 156eb4a...f938e68 main       -> origin/main  (forced update)
# Already up to date.
git push
#    f938e68..74ed234  main -> main
git log --oneline origin/main
# 74ed234 Add coupon field
# 156eb4a Add debug free-shipping flag
# f938e68 Add checkout

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
# Lina
git revert --no-edit HEAD
# [main a2dbf7d] Revert "Add debug free-shipping flag"
#  1 file changed, 1 deletion(-)
#  delete mode 100644 flags.js
git push
#    45919d6..a2dbf7d  main -> main
# Omar, later that day
git pull --rebase
# Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/main.
git log --oneline
# 452ade0 Add coupon field
# a2dbf7d Revert "Add debug free-shipping flag"
# 45919d6 Add debug free-shipping flag
# 1d03087 Add checkout

content.text: The first tab is the hook, reproduced. Omar's pull printed
because, from his clone's point of view, the remote had simply fallen behind: his
. His next push was an ordinary fast-forward, and it carried
. In the second tab the flag's file is gone for both of them, the revert sits in the history next to the mistake, and nobody needed
. Commit IDs differ between tabs because each scenario ran in a fresh repository.
